extracted.intended_audience: startup founders, CEOs, people & culture leads, internal/employee comms managers and startup managers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for building and running effective internal communications at startups, spanning leader training, recurring messaging, meeting formats for cross-team knowledge-sharing, crisis preparedness, and compassionate transition messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal comms is a two-way street
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal comms requires both top-down clarity and open channels for frontline feedback: you need to deliver crystal-clear messaging that resonates with employees and also open opportunities for employees to give valuable feedback from the frontlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt practices to company size and distribution; two-way communication fortifies product and company building, increases engagement, helps retain talent, and prevents misunderstandings, conflict, and product crises. Emphasize both clarity of leadership messaging and mechanisms that let employees report concerns, ideas, and context back up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach your leaders to fish (and other tactics to boost internal PR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest in internal comms expertise and train leaders to be communicators: hire someone who specializes in internal/employee comms, equip leaders with concise tools (cliff notes) and teach them how to cascade messages effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hire a dedicated internal comms pro; roll out a weekly(ish) email for leaders that summarizes 'things to know, things to do, things to share' so leaders can cascade information. Use leader-facing materials to save leaders’ time and make them better communicators. Create micro-moments (e.g., small weekly CEO coffee slots where six people sign up) to give face time and surface diverse perspectives. Use these tactics to ensure messages are understood and to surface dissonance early (employees will 'call bullshit' faster than external audiences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Send these two crucial emails every week — no exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain relentless cadence and structure in written internal updates: one regular update to the entire company and another weekly note to direct reports outlining goals for the week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Front: the company-wide email (e.g., 'Revenue update') should be consistent in structure, cadence and send-time, transparently sharing metrics and what's working/what's not to create accountability. The direct-reports email (e.g., 'Goals for the week') should list what the leader is focusing on so managers understand priorities and how time is spent; making calendars public and sharing decks about a leader’s work can complement this. Regularity signals priorities and enforces accountability even if it takes time to write. Share the good, the bad, and the ugly to avoid excuses or distraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set out the welcome mat for exploration and host Open Houses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use flexible, small-group forums (Open Houses) anyone can announce to share dynamic topics that don't warrant a full All Hands — these can be Q&A sessions, slides+discussion, demos, or research presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always clarify who the Open House is for and its objectives in the invite so people can decide whether to attend. Use Open Houses to surface niche topics, reinforce All Hands themes, present insights (user segments, prototypes, research, progress narratives), build cross-office connections, and give more people a seat at the table. If many Open Houses converge on a topic, consider adding it to the next All Hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t shy from contrarian opinions and candid feedback — invite them to the table (Contrarian Office Hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create structured, time-bounded forums that explicitly invite critique and contrarian views (e.g., weekly 'Contrarian Office Hours') where anyone can raise issues, ideas, or grievances without personal attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the session to be time-limited (about an hour), collect questions/topics in advance so leadership can prepare, and budget time per question. Log every issue raised on an internal wiki as action items with owners and status to ensure follow-up and accountability. End sessions by celebrating wins to balance critique. Make attendance or exposure part of new-hire onboarding to signal cultural importance. Leadership must meaningfully respond and take action where appropriate to maintain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent communication wildfires by creating a culture of preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Build systems and norms to surface and triage early signals of incidents so small problems are raised and handled before they escalate into crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Flag early, flag often' — empower everyone to raise incidents (describe, don't analyze) in a dedicated channel. Adopt a simple incident-classification system (inspired by the National Fire Danger Rating System) with color/level triggers, and adapt thresholds to your company’s stage, industry, and risk tolerance. Triage raised issues with the appropriate technical/support teams. Crucially, thank people who flag incidents (even false alarms) to encourage reporting and avoid creating a culture where raising concerns is punished or risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage top-down decisions and transitions with compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: When planning major transitions (role changes, strategy shifts, executive moves), be highly intentional about internal messaging: plan rollout, give space for employee reflection and Q&A, and communicate with human vulnerability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan announcements well in advance with cofounders, board, and head of comms; iterate on tone and context. Time the announcement to allow processing (e.g., don't drop big news right before weekend), offer follow-up sessions (Q&A, anonymous question collection, all-hands, informal gatherings) and update people over multiple touchpoints. Be transparent about ongoing involvement/role changes and allow leaders to show emotion and vulnerability — this helps employees process change and maintain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat employees as your number-one audience and leverage internal buy-in for external PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize employees as the primary audience for company storytelling and messaging because internal resonance often predicts external resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tap into employees’ vested interest to help tell your story externally; if your story doesn't resonate internally, it likely won't externally. Strengthen culture via accountability, authenticity, clear goals, and two-way communication rather than relying solely on perks and benefits to drive engagement.
